newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says single currency will go ahead on time.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says single currency will go ahead on time.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Sunday he never doubted Europe's planned single currency, the euro, would be launched on time in 1999 and his Group of Seven (G7) partners did not doubt its punctual launch.

Kohl, attending a meeting of the seven most industrialised nations (G7) in Denver, United States, came under heavy fire at home this weekend from industry leaders and trade unions over his government's failure to tackle rising unemployment.

But in an interview with ZDF television he said his trip to Denver had, among other things, shown him that Germans had to be more flexible when seeking a job and he brushed aside doubts European economic and monetary union (EMU) would come on time.
"I have never doubted this...My (G7) colleagues are in absolutely no doubt about this," Kohl told ZDF's Bonn Direkt programme according to a transcript of the interview which was released in Bonn.

Kohl blamed the German mentality, saying Germans were not flexible enough, but he also cast doubt over whether they would be more successful in finding jobs even if they were prepared move away to other towns like Americans.
"We can learn a lot from the Americans in the way that they have developed a more dynamic situation. They are more flexible, more spontaneous and more mobile," Kohl said.
"If you have no job, you can see this clearly in Denver, then you go somewhere else. But this thinking is simply impossible in Germany," Kohl said.

Doubts are growing among the leaders of Kohl's coalition partner, the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), as to whether EMU will be launched on time since the new left-wing government came to power in France.
They say the switch to the single currency could mean monetary suicide for Germany after new French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin suggested it could be launched with softer financial criteria.
Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber of the CSU said on Saturday EMU should only go ahead if all participants strictly met the Maastricht convergence criteria for the 1999 launch.
Huber is one of many leading figures in the CSU, Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats, who advocate a delay to swapping Germany's mark for a potentially weaker euro.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, the chairman of the BDI industry federation, launched a sharp attack on the German government for diluting a tax reform bill aimed at providing more incentives to invest in Germany.

Henkel was one of a chorus of industry leaders who initally supported the reform but have recently accused the ruling coalition of retreating from their ambitious tax goals by baulking at unpopular, but necessary measures.

Kohl and his government also faced a barrage of criticism from trade unions, politicians and economists, and Klaus Zwickel, the head of Germany's largest union, IG Metall, called on them to admit defeat and step down.
The G7 meeting ended on Sunday.
